visual_goal: Show the reliance chain as a stacked structure: general IT controls form the foundation that makes application controls and system-generated reports reliable, which feed process controls and financial statement assertions; entity-level controls sit over the foundation.
prompt: A building-like stacked illustration, drawn as a small temple seen from the front. At the very top, a roof band labeled 'Financial statement assertions'. Under the roof, three pillars side by side: the left pillar labeled 'Application controls', the middle pillar labeled 'Key reports', the right pillar labeled 'Process controls'. A small arrow goes from 'Key reports' sideways into 'Process controls', labeled 'feed'. The pillars stand on a wide, solid foundation slab made of four stone blocks side by side, labeled 'Logical access', 'Change management', 'IT operations' and 'Program development', with a band across the whole slab labeled 'General IT controls'. Two upward arrows labeled 'make reliable' rise from the slab into the 'Application controls' pillar and the 'Key reports' pillar. Beneath the slab, a broad base step labeled 'Entity-level controls'. On the right of the image, a small inset shows the same temple with one foundation block cracked and the pillars above it tilting, to show that a failed foundation takes everything above with it.
alt: A temple-like structure: entity-level controls and a foundation of four general IT control blocks support pillars for application controls, key reports and process controls, which hold up the financial statement assertions; an inset shows a cracked foundation tilting everything above.

visual_goal: Show the payout rule lifecycle: Draft, Submitted, then Rejected or Approved by a different person, then Scheduled or straight to Active, and finally Superseded but kept, never overwritten.
prompt: A state path drawn as smooth, plain rounded stepping stones from left to right: 'Draft', then 'Submitted', then 'Approved', then 'Active', then 'Superseded'. Each stone carries only its one label. Between 'Submitted' and 'Approved' stand two different unlabeled people, one handing a blank paper to the other, showing that the approver is not the author. From 'Submitted' a short grey side path drops down to an end stone 'Rejected'. Between 'Approved' and 'Active' the path forks: one path goes straight into 'Active', and a second path curves above through a stone 'Scheduled' with a small blank calendar-page icon, then down into 'Active'. The 'Superseded' stone sits on a small shelf holding a row of plain blank folders, showing old versions are kept. In total exactly seven arrows: Draft to Submitted, Submitted to Rejected, Submitted to Approved, Approved to Active, Approved to Scheduled, Scheduled to Active, Active to Superseded.
alt: A payout rule moves from Draft to Submitted, is rejected or approved by a different person, becomes Active directly or via Scheduled, and is finally Superseded and archived rather than overwritten.

visual_goal: Show a payout rule change after remediation: analyst proposes, approver approves, the rule store publishes a version to the payout engine, and every step drops its own record into the evidence store, with each payout carrying its rule version.
prompt: A left-to-right flow along an upper track with a long evidence vault running underneath. Upper track, left to right: an unlabeled person at a desk next to a box 'Analyst', one arrow labeled 'override 12%' into a cabinet labeled 'Rule store'; from 'Rule store' one arrow up-right to a second unlabeled person with a box 'Approver', and one arrow from 'Approver' back into 'Rule store' with a check mark; then one arrow from 'Rule store' right to a machine with gears labeled 'Payout engine', and the arrow carries a small tag 'rule version'. Out of the 'Payout engine' come a few coins, each with the same small tag. Underneath the whole track, a long locked vault labeled 'Evidence store'. Three short dotted arrows drop down into the vault, each carrying a sealed receipt: one from 'Rule store' after the proposal, one from 'Rule store' after the approval, and one from 'Payout engine'.
alt: An analyst proposes a 12% override in the rule store, an approver approves it, the rule store publishes a rule version to the payout engine, and each step drops a sealed record into an evidence store below.

visual_goal: Show the remediation architecture: three change paths (code, rules, emergency) each with its own separation of duties, all reaching SFP production and all feeding one evidence store that control monitoring and the auditor read.
prompt: A left-to-right illustration with three horizontal lanes, each a straight chain of boxes joined by single arrows. Top lane, labeled 'Code', a chain of four: box 'Author and reviewer' (two small figures), arrow, box 'Repository', arrow, conveyor belt 'Pipeline', arrow, server tower 'SFP production'. Middle lane, labeled 'Rules', a chain of three: box 'Maker and checker' (two small figures), arrow, cabinet 'Rule store', arrow, into the same server tower 'SFP production'. Bottom lane, labeled 'Emergency', a chain of three: box 'On-call' (one small figure), arrow, stopwatch box 'Break-glass', dashed orange arrow, into the same server tower 'SFP production'. The server tower is tall and spans all three lanes on the right. At the far left, a box 'Identity provider' with thin plain lines to the three lanes. Beneath the lanes, a wide locked vault labeled 'Evidence store'. Exactly four short straight vertical arrows drop into the vault: one from 'Pipeline', one from 'Rule store', one from 'Break-glass', one from the bottom of 'SFP production'. To the right of the vault, one arrow into a dashboard 'Control monitoring', then one arrow into a clipboard 'Auditor'. In total exactly fourteen arrows. The only words in the image are the quoted labels.
alt: Three change paths, for code via repository and pipeline, rules via a rule store, and emergencies via break-glass, all reach SFP production; each path and production feed one evidence store, read by control monitoring and the auditor.
